patient.chief_complaint: Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy with fever and urinary symptoms — urosepsis as precipitant
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. T. is a 55-year-old Black woman with hepatitis B cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) and prior hepatic encephalopathy who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter for worsening confusion over the past 36 hours. The daughter arrived for her daily check and found her mother disoriented — she could not remember the current year and was confused about her location. The daughter also noted her mother had been complaining of pain with urination and lower abdominal pain for 5 days but had self-medicated with cranberry juice and refused to call her doctor. On arrival the patient has a temperature of 38.6°C, heart rate 114, and blood pressure 106/62 — consistent with sepsis physiology. Right lower quadrant tenderness and right loin pain are present. Urinalysis shows 2+ bacteria, 2+ WBC, positive nitrites, and positive leukocyte esterase — confirming a urinary tract infection. In the setting of hepatitis B cirrhosis with already compromised hepatic urea cycle function, a systemic urinary tract infection (UTI) with early urosepsis provides the inflammatory trigger that dramatically raises ammonia production and precipitates overt HE. The ammonia on admission is 156 µmol/L — markedly elevated. EEG shows the classic hepatic encephalopathy pattern. CT head excludes structural causes. Ascites requires paracentesis to exclude concurrent SBP.

critical_actions: IV ceftriaxone for E. coli urosepsis — treat the HE precipitant
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude concurrent SBP (cannot rely on clinical exam in cirrhosis with fever)
Lactulose titrated to 2-3 stools/day — not maximum purging
Correct hypokalemia — potassium worsens HE via renal ammoniagenesis
Transplant referral — MELD 18 + two overt HE episodes + HCC within Milan criteria = multiple indications
Address HBV DNA viremia — counsel on tenofovir adherence (no resistance found)
contraindicated_actions: Defer paracentesis assuming UTI is the only infection: In decompensated cirrhosis with fever, SBP and UTI can coexist; paracentesis is always required to exclude SBP when patient has ascites and encephalopathy
Use fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) empirically without culture results: Rising E. coli resistance rates in hospitalized cirrhotic patients — ceftriaxone is preferred empiric choice in sepsis
Avoid lactulose to prevent diarrhea-induced hypokalemia: Lactulose is essential — titrate to 2-3 stools/day; omitting lactulose in grade 3 HE worsens prognosis
teaching_pearls: Urosepsis is a common but underrecognized HE precipitant — always check urinalysis in encephalopathic cirrhotics
Paracentesis is required whenever cirrhotic ascites patient has fever or encephalopathy — cannot clinically exclude SBP
Hypokalemia worsens hepatic encephalopathy through renal ammoniagenesis — K+ correction is part of HE treatment
HBV DNA detectable on tenofovir almost always reflects adherence failure, not resistance — check before switching drugs
HCC within Milan criteria + cirrhosis = candidate for liver transplant with MELD exception points
key_reasoning_points: Urosepsis precipitates HE through two mechanisms: (1) systemic cytokines impair hepatic urea cycle function; (2) infection-driven catabolism increases peripheral glutamine/ammonia production
SBP and UTI can coexist in cirrhosis with ascites — always perform paracentesis when ascites is present and encephalopathy is unexplained
Hypokalemia worsens HE by increasing renal ammoniagenesis — H+/K+ exchange in renal tubules shifts ammonium production; correction of K+ reduces ammonia
Detectable HBV DNA on tenofovir: resistance is rare; first check adherence. No resistance found confirms medication failure.
HCC within Milan criteria independently qualifies for liver transplant and receives MELD exception points — discuss dual indications (HCC + recurrent HE) with transplant team
